title: Cider Production
one_liner: A small, flavor-led beverage alcohol niche where craft producers and Angry Orchard compete for limited shelf space while cider tries to hold roughly 1% of the broader beer-adjacent market.
overview: Cider producers ferment apples, pears and other fruit into alcoholic cider and may also sell soft cider, perry, apple cider vinegar and seasonal specialty products. The industry is fragmented, regionally distributed and tied to orchard supply, packaging, distributor access and alcohol regulation. The post-2010 boom created a national cider shelf, led by Angry Orchard, but the category has matured into a craft-heavy niche competing with beer, flavored malt beverages, hard seltzer, wine and spirits RTDs. In 2025, retail scanner data showed a return to low-single-digit growth, while TTB production data showed a lower domestic production base than the 2023 peak.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 producer revenue estimate: about $603 million; 2025 measured off-premise hard cider retail sales: $502 million
key_stats.growth: 2025 hard cider sales growth: +2.0% in Circana measured channels and +1.6% in NIQ data
key_stats.production: 2025 US hard cider production: 21.7 million wine gallons, down from 29.4 million wine gallons in 2023
key_stats.taxable_withdrawals: 2025 US hard cider taxable withdrawals: 34.8 million wine gallons, down from 37.4 million in 2024 and 40.1 million in 2023
key_stats.business_base: 2025 TTB wine industry members: 8,785 total wine premises; 856 premises reported hard cider production
key_stats.retail_share: 2026 industry commentary expects hard cider to remain around 1% of the beer market

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022 producer revenue estimate: $529.0 million, derived from the baseline report's 2021 revenue of $517.6 million and its 2021-2026 CAGR forecast of +2.2%
baseline_2022.production: 2022 US hard cider production: 29.3 million wine gallons
baseline_2022.taxable_withdrawals: 2022 US hard cider taxable withdrawals: 41.3 million wine gallons
baseline_2022.context: The 2022 baseline followed a 2021 market of $517.6 million, 1,385 enterprises, 2,036 employees and a 3.6% profit margin in the source file.

how_it_makes_money.primary_revenue: Selling packaged and draft alcoholic cider through beer and wine wholesalers into grocery, mass, convenience, liquor, club, bar and restaurant channels.
how_it_makes_money.secondary_revenue: Taproom and orchard sales, limited releases, cider clubs, direct-to-consumer where legal, contract production, perry, soft cider and apple cider vinegar.
how_it_makes_money.pricing_model: Revenue is driven by case volume, package mix, distributor terms, brand velocity, seasonal releases and premium craft pricing.
how_it_makes_money.demand_drivers: Flavor innovation, gluten-free positioning, local craft appeal, apple harvest quality, alcohol spending, retail shelf space and on-premise availability.

cost_structure.fruit_and_inputs: Apples, pear juice, concentrates, yeast, sugar, adjunct fruit, spices and flavorings are core variable costs; 2025-26 apple supply is ample, with USApple forecasting 278.5 million bushels for the 2025/26 crop year.
cost_structure.packaging: Cans, bottles, cartons, labels, kegs and case packaging are material costs; 2025 TTB standards-of-fill changes added 16 oz and 19.2 oz wine/cider package flexibility.
cost_structure.labor: Orchard, cellar, packaging, compliance, sales and hospitality labor are meaningful costs, with USApple citing high grower labor costs in 2025.
cost_structure.distribution_and_freight: Three-tier distribution margins, freight, cold storage and regional delivery limit small producers' scale economics.
cost_structure.marketing_and_trade_spend: Brand building, tastings, festivals, seasonal launches, retailer programming and distributor incentives matter because cider has limited shelf space.
cost_structure.tax_and_compliance: TTB wine-premises compliance, formula approvals for flavored products, state alcohol rules and federal excise taxes shape product design; qualifying still hard cider is taxed at 22.6 cents per wine gallon.
cost_structure.profitability: Baseline file profit margin was 3.6% in 2021 and forecast at 3.4% in 2026, reflecting small-scale production and high competition.

current_dynamics: The category stabilized in 2025 after 2024 declines, with measured retail sales rising modestly even as TTB data showed domestic hard cider production dropping to 21.7 million wine gallons. Growth is concentrated in flavor-forward, light, gluten-free and craft offerings, while the core apple cider set faces low innovation perceptions, shelf constraints and competition from hard seltzers, FMBs and spirits RTDs. Tariffs, orchard weather events and state alcohol-tax debates are adding cost and policy pressure in 2025-2026.
whats_growing: 2025 fruit-flavored ciders including mango, raspberry, blueberry, orange, berry blends and imperial seasonal releases
2025 light and lower-calorie ciders that fit wellness-driven alcohol occasions
2025 regional craft cider brands with local orchard stories and taproom followings
2025 gluten-free positioning as a differentiator against beer and flavored malt beverages
2026 trade education, lobbying and technical programming around CiderCon and ACA advocacy
whats_shrinking: 2025 domestic hard cider production volume, down to 21.7 million wine gallons from 29.4 million in 2023
2025 taxable hard cider withdrawals, down to 34.8 million wine gallons from 37.4 million in 2024
Large-format undifferentiated apple-only offerings where shelf velocity is weak
Retail shelf space for cider as RTDs, hard seltzers and FMBs compete for the same cold-box placements
Margins for small producers facing packaging, labor, distribution and compliance costs
recent_developments: 2025-07-22: The Bubble Tax Modernization Act was reintroduced in the House as H.R. 4613 to raise allowable carbonation levels for cider, mead and fruit wine.
2025-08-15: USApple forecast the 2025/26 US apple crop at 278.5 million bushels, up 1.3% from 2024/25 and 3.6% above the five-year average.
2025-12-28: Circana measured US hard cider sales at $502 million for the 52 weeks ending Dec. 28, 2025, up 2.0%, with Angry Orchard up 3.6%.
2026-02-24: Boston Beer reported 2025 net revenue of $1.965 billion, down 2.4%, with growth in Angry Orchard partly offsetting declines in other brands.
2026-06-03: TTB updated wine data showing 2025 hard cider production at 21.7 million wine gallons and 2025 hard cider taxable withdrawals at 34.8 million wine gallons.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is modest rather than boom-like. Cider should benefit from flavor innovation, gluten-free demand, local craft storytelling and ample 2025/26 apple supply, but the category is unlikely to break out without better shelf productivity and stronger consumer recruitment. Expect low-single-digit sales growth or flat performance in measured retail channels, continued pressure on smaller producers' margins, more fruit-forward limited releases and continued lobbying for carbonation and package-size rules that fit modern cider formats.

title: Cigar Lounges
one_liner: Cigar lounges sell premium cigars, drinks, memberships and social smoking space to adult consumers in a fragmented, regulation-heavy leisure niche.
overview: Cigar lounges are specialty venues where adult customers buy and smoke cigars on site, often alongside whiskey, cocktails, coffee, food, private lockers, events and memberships. The industry sits between tobacco retail and hospitality: operators need humidified inventory, trained tobacconists, compliant ventilation and, in many markets, separate tobacco, liquor and indoor-smoking permissions. Demand recovered from the 2020 shutdown period and has shifted toward experience-led, premium occasions rather than high-volume tobacco consumption. The market remains highly fragmented in 2025, with most locations independent and single-site, while Casa de Montecristo is the most visible multi-location brand.

key_stats.market_size: $1.2 billion US cigar lounge revenue in 2025, estimated by Avvale citing IBISWorld 2025 analysis
key_stats.growth: 5.2% CAGR over 2020-2025, estimated by Avvale citing IBISWorld 2025 analysis

key_stats.premium_cigar_imports: 429.8 million premium large cigars imported into the US in 2025, down 0.1% from 2024, per Cigar Association of America
key_stats.total_cigar_consumption: Approximately 9.9 billion US cigars consumed in 2025, down modestly from 2024, per Cigar Association of America
key_stats.adult_use: 8.6 million US adults smoked cigars in 2021; 2023 exclusive adult cigar smoking was 2.0%, per CDC/MMWR
key_stats.typical_startup_cost: $150,000-$750,000 US startup cost in 2025-2026 planning benchmarks, with ventilation commonly $20,000-$50,000, per Avvale

baseline_2022.market_size: $840.0 million in 2022, estimated from baseline IBISWorld 2021 revenue of $821.9 million and its 2021-2026 projected 2.2% CAGR
baseline_2022.growth: 2.2% projected 2022 growth based on baseline IBISWorld 2021-2026 CAGR
baseline_2022.establishments: About 2,104 establishments in 2022, estimated from baseline 2021 establishments of 2,107 and projected 2021-2027 CAGR of -0.16%
baseline_2022.enterprises: About 1,913 enterprises in 2022, estimated from baseline 2021 enterprises of 1,920 and projected 2021-2027 CAGR of -0.35%
baseline_2022.employment: About 4,167 workers in 2022, estimated from baseline 2021 employment of 4,101 and projected 2021-2027 CAGR of 1.60%

how_it_makes_money.cigars_and_tobacco: 2021 baseline: 65.1% of revenue from cigars and other tobacco products; 2025 operators still rely on premium sticks, boxes and in-lounge markups.
how_it_makes_money.beverages: 2021 baseline: 13.4% of revenue from beverages; 2025-2026 full-service lounges use whiskey, bourbon, cocktails and pairing programs to lift average tickets where liquor rules permit.
how_it_makes_money.food: 2021 baseline: 7.0% of revenue from food; contribution varies by local separation rules for smoking and food service.
how_it_makes_money.accessories_other: 2021 baseline: 14.5% from accessories and other sales such as cutters, lighters, humidors, lockers, memberships and events.
how_it_makes_money.memberships_events: 2025-2026 independent planning benchmarks put memberships at 5-10% of revenue and private events/classes at 5-10% for diversified lounges.

cost_structure.inventory: Cigar, beverage and food inventory are core variable costs; 2025 planning benchmarks cite blended COGS near 40% for a full-service lounge model.
cost_structure.labor: Staffing for tobacconists, managers, servers and bartenders is often the second-largest operating cost; 2025 planning benchmarks use 25-30% of gross sales for staffing.
cost_structure.occupancy: Rent is highly location-sensitive because affluent urban and tourist districts drive traffic but raise fixed costs.
cost_structure.compliance_and_capex: 2025-2026 startup benchmarks cite $15,000-$60,000 for a walk-in humidor and $20,000-$50,000 for dedicated ventilation and filtration.
cost_structure.licenses_insurance: Tobacco retail permits, on-premise smoking exemptions, liquor licenses, health permits and liquor/general liability insurance add recurring compliance costs.
cost_structure.profit: Baseline IBISWorld profit margin was 5.1% in 2021 and projected 6.2% in 2026; 2025-2026 small-business benchmarks often cite 10-25% net margins for well-run operators, depending on alcohol, memberships and rent.

current_dynamics: The 2025-2026 market is healthier in dollars than in unit volume. Total US cigar consumption was about 9.9 billion units in 2025, but lower-priced large cigars are declining while premium imports held around 430 million units. That mix favors lounges because their economics depend on premium selection, atmosphere, pairing occasions and repeat customers rather than mass-market volume. The biggest constraints are local indoor-smoking rules, tobacco taxes, liquor licensing delays, ventilation costs, e-commerce price competition and public-health pressure on flavored and youth-oriented cigar products.
whats_growing: Premium and higher-value cigars: 2025 imports of large cigars priced above $0.76 rose 3%, while premium large cigar imports stayed near 429.8 million units.
Memberships, private lockers and recurring club models: 2025-2026 planning benchmarks place memberships at 5-10% of revenue for full-service lounges and 40-50% for membership-first clubs.
Cigar-and-spirits pairings: 2025-2026 lounge models rely on alcohol and beverages for 20-30% of revenue where licensing allows.
Online discovery and cigar education: 2024 online cigar/cigarillo distribution was expected to grow at an 8.9% CAGR for 2025-2033, raising the importance of local search and events for lounges.
Nicaraguan supply: premium cigar imports from Nicaragua reached 258.4 million units in 2025, up from 253.1 million in 2024.
whats_shrinking: Low-priced large cigars: 2025 imports below $0.15 fell 6% and the $0.15-$0.229 tier fell 9%.
Total large-cigar import volume: 2025 large cigar imports fell to 7.77 billion units, down 6% from 2024.
Domestic cigar output: 2025 Cigar Association of America summaries cite another decline in US domestic cigar production based on TTB taxable removals.
Youth cigar use: CDC reported 330,000 middle and high school cigar users in 2024 versus 420,000 in 2023, reducing long-term category replacement but easing some public-health pressure.
Single-revenue tobacco-only formats: 2025-2026 planning benchmarks warn cigar-only lounges are weaker than models with alcohol, memberships and events.
recent_developments: 2024-08: Gurkha Cigar Group launched the Fantasma limited-edition cigar for Texas retailer Spec's, signaling retailer-specific premium releases.
2025-01: The D.C. Circuit upheld vacatur of FDA's deeming rule as applied to premium cigars, while remanding for refinement of the premium-cigar definition.
2025-09: Casa de Montecristo announced new West Palm Beach and Chicago-area partner locations, expanding its national branded lounge footprint.
2025-12: Cigar Association of America estimated 2025 US cigar consumption at about 9.9 billion units, with premium cigars around 460 million units.
2026-04: A D.C. district court again left premium cigars outside the FDA Deeming Rule under the court-defined premium category, according to industry reporting.
outlook: Through 2026, cigar lounges should remain a modest-growth, high-touch consumer services niche rather than a mass-market tobacco story. Revenue is likely to keep outpacing unit consumption because premium cigars, beverage pairings, lockers, events and memberships raise spend per visit. Best-positioned operators will be in high-income metro, tourism and business districts with permissive cigar-bar rules and liquor access. Risks remain material: state and city smoking restrictions, excise taxes, insurance, high buildout costs, and online cigar retail can pressure traffic and margins. A reasonable 2026 industry range is about $1.2 billion-$1.3 billion in US lounge revenue, assuming 2025 estimated revenue of $1.2 billion and continued mid-single-digit nominal growth.
one_sentence: In 2025, US cigar lounges were an estimated $1.2 billion industry, supported by resilient premium cigar demand, bar and membership revenue, and the continued appeal of dedicated indoor-smoking venues where state and local rules allow them.

title: Civic, Social & Youth Organizations in the US
one_liner: Member-based civic clubs, social associations and youth groups are rebuilding in-person engagement while competing with digital communities and episodic volunteering.
overview: Civic, Social & Youth Organizations in the US includes establishments that promote the civic and social interests of members, including alumni associations, parent-teacher and booster groups, fraternal lodges, ethnic associations, veterans' membership organizations, scouting organizations and social clubs. The 2022 IBIS baseline described a mature-to-declining industry because in-person club membership, volunteer hours and legacy youth organizations had weakened before COVID-19 and were hit again by event closures. By 2025, public market estimates show revenue above the 2022 baseline as in-person events, corporate giving, household wealth and nonprofit program activity recovered, but the demand model is different: members want flexible commitments, hybrid participation, visible impact and lower-friction ways to contribute.

key_stats.growth: 2025: 5.3% average annual revenue growth over the prior 5 years, reflecting recovery from pandemic lows and inflation-supported nominal revenue.

key_stats.charitable_giving: 2025: total US charitable giving reached $617.2 billion, up 5.7% from 2024 in current dollars and 3.0% after inflation.
key_stats.public_society_benefit_giving: 2024: public-society benefit organizations received $66.84 billion, up 19.5% in current dollars.

how_it_makes_money.membership_dues: 2022: membership services accounted for 22.7% of revenue, led by annual dues and member access fees.
how_it_makes_money.donations_and_grants: 2022: private gifts, grants and donations accounted for 21.5% of revenue; 2024 total US charitable giving rose 6.3% to $592.50 billion and 2025 giving rose 5.7% to $617.2 billion.
how_it_makes_money.events_and_facilities: 2022: prepared meals and beverages accounted for 14.9%, gaming services 6.5%, and rental of nonresidential space 1.3%, making in-person attendance a key monetization lever.
how_it_makes_money.government_support: 2022: government grants and support accounted for 4.9% of revenue.
how_it_makes_money.program_and_merchandise_fees: 2024: major youth organizations showed continued reliance on program services and inventory sales, with Girl Scouts USA reporting $50.47 million in program-service revenue and $24.06 million in net inventory sales.

cost_structure.labor: 2022: IBIS baseline wages were $4.673 billion; 2025 market benchmarks reported average pay per employee of $25,788.
cost_structure.program_delivery: 2022: event staffing, volunteer coordination, youth programming, insurance, safeguarding, training, supplies and facility operations were core operating costs tied to in-person service delivery.
cost_structure.food_beverage_and_event_inputs: 2022: meals, beverages and gaming represented 21.4% of revenue, so food purchasing, licensing, event logistics and compliance costs remained meaningful for clubs with facilities.
cost_structure.administration_and_professional_services: 2025: market benchmarks reported professional services at 4.2% of expenses, reflecting audit, legal, fundraising, technology and compliance needs.
cost_structure.technology: 2023: 18% of formal volunteers served at least partly online, pushing organizations to fund CRM, online renewal, virtual volunteering and digital fundraising tools.
cost_structure.margin: 2022: IBIS baseline profit margin was 5.3%, leaving small organizations exposed to wage, rent, insurance and fundraising volatility.

major_players: Scouting America: 2024 revenue was $330.3 million in the national organization Form 990 data, and the Boy Scouts of America name change became effective on February 8, 2025.
Girl Scouts of the United States of America: FY2025 revenue was $148.8 million, with contributions at 35.4% and program services at 33.0% of total revenue.

YMCA of the USA and affiliated YMCAs: Forbes listed 2024 aggregate total revenue of $9.2 billion, though much of the system also overlaps recreation, childcare and health services rather than pure NAICS 813410.
Rotary International and The Rotary Foundation: global civic-service network headquartered in Illinois, with Rotary reporting more than $3 billion invested in projects over the prior 100 years.
Lions Clubs International: 2026 public profile reports 1.4 million members in 50,000 clubs globally, with the US headquarters in Illinois.
Kiwanis International: legacy service-club network with exposure to the same aging-membership and chapter-renewal pressures as Rotary and Lions.
current_dynamics: The 2025 market looks healthier in nominal dollars than the 2022 IBIS baseline because in-person programs resumed and 2024-2025 philanthropy improved. The demand problem is structural rather than cyclical: 2023 formal volunteering recovered to 28.3%, but average annual volunteer hours per volunteer fell to 70 in 2023 from 96.5 in 2017, showing a shift toward shorter and more episodic participation. Organizations that translate civic identity into flexible events, youth leadership, local service and digital renewals are gaining share of attention; legacy clubs that depend on fixed meeting schedules and older member cohorts keep losing relevance.
whats_growing: 2025: nominal revenue, supported by a 2025 estimate of $26.8 billion and 5.3% average annual growth over the prior 5 years.
2025: charitable funding tailwinds, with total US giving up 5.7% to $617.2 billion.
2023: formal volunteering participation, up to 75.7 million people and 28.3% of the age-16+ population from 23.2% in 2021.
2023: hybrid and virtual volunteering, with 18% of formal volunteers serving fully or partly online.
2024: public-society benefit giving, up 19.5% in current dollars to $66.84 billion.
2025: youth-organization repositioning around inclusion, digital renewal and family-friendly program access.
whats_shrinking: 2025: business counts, with IBISWorld reporting 23,250 businesses and a 0.2% decline from 2024.
2023: volunteer intensity, with average formal volunteer hours down to 70 hours in 2023 versus 96.5 hours in 2017.
2022: legacy membership dependence, with IBIS identifying long-term declines at service clubs and youth organizations as a core industry threat.
2024: traditional bequest giving, down 1.6% in current dollars and 4.4% after inflation.
2025: small local chapters that cannot recruit younger members, maintain volunteers or absorb insurance, rent and compliance costs.
recent_developments: 2024-05-07: Boy Scouts of America announced it would rebrand as Scouting America, effective 2025-02-08.
2024-11-19: Census and AmeriCorps released 2023 CEV data showing formal volunteering recovered to 75.7 million people and 28.3% of the age-16+ population.
2025-02-08: Scouting America became the official name of the former Boy Scouts of America on its 115th anniversary.
2025-04: IBISWorld's public industry page listed 23,250 Civic, Social & Youth Organizations businesses in 2025, down 0.2% from 2024.
2025-06: Giving USA reported 2024 US charitable giving of $592.50 billion, up 6.3% in current dollars.
2026-07: Giving USA 2026 coverage reported 2025 US charitable giving of $617.2 billion, up 5.7% in current dollars.
outlook: Through 2026, the industry should remain modestly positive in nominal revenue but uneven in real participation. Giving and sponsorship are supportive after 2024-2025 gains, and the 2023 volunteer rebound suggests community demand survived the pandemic. The limiting factors are weaker recurring membership, lower volunteer hours per person, aging service-club cohorts, youth-program competition from sports and digital entertainment, and local cost pressure. The strongest operators will package membership around measurable community impact, youth leadership, family events, hybrid participation and simple annual renewal; weaker clubs will consolidate, close chapters or rely more heavily on episodic fundraisers.
themes: Competition from digital communities and youth sports
data_year: 2026 with 2025 market and giving data, 2024 nonprofit filings, 2023 Census/AmeriCorps civic-engagement data, and 2022 IBIS baseline data
one_sentence: The industry is a fragmented nonprofit and membership-service market funded by dues, donations, events, grants, food and beverage sales, and program fees, with 2025 revenue estimated at $26.8 billion after a post-pandemic rebound but with traditional membership still under pressure.

title: Classic Car Dealers
one_liner: Classic car dealers sell, consign, restore and sometimes auction collectible vehicles, with demand tied to wealth, nostalgia, credit conditions and online marketplace competition.
overview: Classic car dealers retail collectible, antique and enthusiast vehicles, typically including cars at least 25 years old, specialty imports, muscle cars, restomods, trucks, SUVs and modern classics from the 1980s through 2000s. Operators buy inventory for resale, sell customer-owned vehicles on consignment, arrange auctions, broker high-value cars, and often add restoration, inspection, storage, transport, financing, warranty or documentation services. The industry is small compared with the broader used-car dealer market, but it handles vehicles with high emotional and investment value. Demand is strongest among affluent collectors and hobbyists, while younger Gen X, millennial and Gen Z buyers are expanding the definition of what counts as collectible.

key_stats.transactions_context: 2025 broad US used-car dealer sector output was $162.055 billion, while classic car dealers represented a small specialty subset
key_stats.online_auction_pressure: Bring a Trailer reported 2025 sales of $1.713 billion from 40,465 sold listings, up 14.3% in sales dollars from 2024
key_stats.collector_base: Hagerty reported in January 2026 that about 43 million US vehicles fit its collector-vehicle definition, equal to roughly 16% of 275 million registered vehicles

baseline_2022.growth: 2022 estimated revenue growth: +8.0%, reflecting the late-pandemic collector-asset boom and elevated auction activity
baseline_2022.source_note: The baseline file directly reports 2020 revenue of $2.155 billion and a 2020-2025 forecast CAGR of -0.6%; the 2022 baseline is an estimate bridged to the later IBIS-cited 2023 market size of $2.8 billion.

how_it_makes_money: Dealers earn money from owned-inventory markups, consignment commissions, auction fees, buyer premiums, restoration and customization work, inspection and appraisal services, financing and warranty referral income, storage, shipping coordination and repeat-customer sourcing mandates. High-end vehicles generate larger gross dollars per sale, while lower-price classics and modern enthusiast cars drive showroom traffic and unit volume.

cost_structure.inventory_and_vehicle_acquisition: Largest cost; capital is tied up in purchased vehicles, reconditioning and carrying costs.
cost_structure.labor: Sales specialists, mechanics, restorers, detailers, photographers, appraisers and administrative staff are important because provenance and condition drive value.
cost_structure.rent_and_showrooms: Showroom, warehouse, storage and event space costs are meaningful for physical dealers.
cost_structure.marketing_and_platform_fees: Online listings, photography, video, auction placement, search ads and marketplace commissions are rising costs.
cost_structure.transport_and_insurance: Enclosed transport, garage liability, consignment insurance and inventory coverage are material costs.
cost_structure.profit: Margins are thin for pure resale but better for restoration, customization, brokerage and services.

current_dynamics: The market in 2025-2026 is split. Online auction platforms and curated marketplaces are still growing volume, but many collector-car price indices have cooled from the 2021-2022 surge. Dealers face customers who can compare prices globally, monitor auction comps in real time and sell directly online. That reduces dealer pricing power unless the dealer can add trust, inspection, financing, provenance, restoration quality or rare sourcing. Demand is most resilient for rare Ferraris, homologation cars, analog supercars, low-mileage modern classics, trucks, SUVs and restomods, while some older mid-market European and traditional blue-chip classics face softer bids.
whats_growing: Online auction and marketplace sales, especially curated listings with deep photography and comment-driven transparency.
1980s, 1990s and 2000s enthusiast vehicles, including analog sports cars, Japanese imports, modern BMW M cars, Corvettes and Porsche models.
Restomods, custom builds and upgraded classics with modern drivetrains, braking, comfort and reliability.
Collector trucks, SUVs and off-road classics such as Broncos, Land Cruisers, Defenders and vintage pickups.
Ancillary services such as appraisal, storage, transport, inspection, documentation and restoration management.
whats_shrinking: Dealer reliance on opaque showroom pricing without transparent comparable sales data.
Speculative buying of ordinary classics that rose sharply during the 2021-2022 boom.
Mid-market vehicles with weak provenance, mediocre restoration quality or large bid-ask gaps.
Traditional dealer-only auctions and local inventory models that cannot compete with national online reach.
Margins on commodity classic inventory as buyers use auction data to negotiate harder.
recent_developments: 2023-09-12: An IBISWorld-cited industry analysis valued the US classic car dealers market, including sales, services and restoration, at $2.8 billion in 2023.
2024-12-09: Hagerty's 2025 Bull Market List said younger enthusiasts were increasingly entering the collector market and that 1980s, 1990s and 2000s vehicles had become collectible.
2025-06-04: Hagerty Market Rating data reported by Classic.com showed the collector market briefly entering flat territory for the first time since 2020 before a modest May 2025 rebound.
2026-01-05: Bring a Trailer reported 2025 gross sales of $1.713 billion from 40,465 sold listings, up 14.3% from 2024.
2026-01-15: Hagerty reported about 43 million US collector vehicles, representing roughly 16% of 275 million registered vehicles.
2026-06-03: FRED/BLS data showed 2025 sectoral output for US used car dealers at $162.055 billion, up from $158.573 billion in 2024.
outlook: Revenue is likely to be roughly flat to slightly down through 2026 unless asset prices reaccelerate. Physical dealers should still win business where trust, inspection, rare sourcing, restoration quality and financing matter, but online auctions will keep pressuring commissions and inventory turns. The healthiest operators will combine showroom credibility with national digital reach, fast comp-based pricing and higher-margin services. The main upside comes from younger buyers redefining collectibility around 1980s-2000s cars, trucks, SUVs and analog performance vehicles; the main downside is a prolonged high-rate environment that keeps discretionary purchases and speculative collector demand subdued.

title: Clothing Alteration Services
one_liner: Small, local tailoring shops alter, repair and refit garments for consumers who need better fit, formalwear adjustments or longer garment life.
overview: Clothing alteration services include hemming, sleeve shortening, waist adjustments, professional and formal attire alterations, and specialty garment repair for items such as leather, wool, cashmere and fur. The 2021 IBISWorld baseline described a low-concentration, low-capital, mature industry dominated by sole proprietors and very small shops, with 2021 revenue of $1.757 billion and 65,333 establishments. Current 2025-2026 public sources suggest the broader U.S. tailoring and alteration services opportunity is larger than the narrow standalone-shop IBIS category, with Deep Market Insights estimating the U.S. market at $2.741 billion in 2025 and a 5.4% CAGR for 2026-2034. Demand is supported by 2025 clothing, footwear and related-services PCE of $586.433 billion, sustainability-oriented repair, occasionwear and premium apparel ownership, while value apparel replacement, store-provided tailoring, dry-cleaner add-ons and scarce skilled labor cap growth.

baseline_2022.note: The baseline file was last updated December 9, 2021, so 2022 is a projection-derived baseline rather than a reported 2022 actual.

core_services: 2021: professional and formal attire alterations represented 31.5% of revenue
2021: specialty garment care and maintenance represented 9.0% of revenue
how_it_makes_money.pricing_model: Per-garment or per-service fees, with higher tickets for bridalwear, suits, leather, fur, designer garments, rush jobs, pickup/delivery and complex reconstruction.
how_it_makes_money.customer_base: Mostly individual consumers, plus boutiques, designers, performers, bridal parties, uniform users and institutions that need fitted apparel.

cost_structure.labor: High labor intensity; skilled sewing and fitting time is the main cost, with 2025 BLS mean pay for tailors, dressmakers and custom sewers at $21.70 per hour.
cost_structure.rent: Storefront rent matters for walk-in shops, especially in dense retail corridors, but many operators reduce overhead through home-based or small-format locations.
cost_structure.materials: Thread, zippers, buttons, interfacing, linings, labels, needles, machine parts and packaging are modest but recurring inputs.
cost_structure.equipment: Low capital requirements; sewing machines, sergers, presses, dress forms and fitting-room fixtures are durable and relatively inexpensive compared with revenue.
cost_structure.marketing_and_platforms: Local search, reviews, appointment software, marketplace fees and pickup/delivery logistics are rising costs for shops that want online discovery.
cost_structure.profitability: 2021 IBISWorld baseline profit margin was 8.3%, with margin pressure from labor availability, rent and low-cost apparel replacement.

current_dynamics: The industry is recovering from the pandemic-era hit to officewear and formalwear but remains structurally fragmented. Eventwear, weddings, luxury resale and sustainability are helping demand for fitting and repair, while casual workwear, cheap imported apparel and apparel retailers' in-house alteration offers reduce traffic for standalone shops. The tight supply of trained tailors is a practical constraint: BLS counted only 13,920 wage-and-salary tailors, dressmakers and custom sewers in 2025, and many industry workers are self-employed or nearing retirement. Digital booking, mobile pickup and ship-in alteration models are growing, but the service still depends heavily on local trust, fitting accuracy and turnaround time.
whats_growing: 2025: premium, bridal, occasionwear and suit alterations, where garment value justifies labor cost
2025: repair and rework services tied to resale, thrift, vintage and sustainability behavior
2025: online booking, pickup/delivery and ship-in alteration models
2025: B2B work for boutiques, designers, costume users, uniforms and local apparel brands
2026: higher-ticket tailoring for luxury, bespoke and custom-fit apparel
whats_shrinking: 2025: basic repairs on very low-cost fast-fashion garments, where replacement is often cheaper than alteration
2025: standalone-shop share of simple hems when department stores, apparel chains and dry cleaners bundle the service
2025: demand tied to daily formal officewear compared with pre-pandemic norms
2025: brick-and-mortar apparel retail adjacency as Census reported clothing and accessories store establishments fell from 143,534 in 2017 to 121,610 in 2022
2026: margins for shops unable to raise prices enough to offset skilled labor and rent costs
recent_developments: 2025-07-08: Census reported U.S. clothing and accessories retail firms fell from 56,731 in 2017 to 52,909 in 2022, while electronic shopping and mail-order firms rose 33% to 44,322.
2026-01-13: BLS reported December 2025 apparel CPI was up 0.6% year over year, with men's suits, sport coats and outerwear down 1.8% year over year and women's dresses down 0.9%.
2026-01-28: FRED/BLS CPS series showed 2025 full-time wage-and-salary employment for tailors, dressmakers and sewers at 21,000 people, excluding self-employed workers.
2026-03-13: Deep Market Insights estimated the U.S. tailoring and alteration services market at $2.741 billion in 2025 and forecast 5.4% CAGR for 2026-2034.
2026-04-09: BEA/FRED data showed 2025 U.S. PCE on clothing, footwear and related services reached $586.433 billion, up from $553.992 billion in 2024.
2026-06-25: BLS May 2025 OEWS reported 13,920 employed tailors, dressmakers and custom sewers with mean annual wage of $45,140.
outlook: Through 2026-2030, revenue should grow modestly for narrow standalone alteration shops and faster for broader tailoring, repair and digital-platform models. Growth depends on consumers continuing to buy higher-value garments, resale apparel needing fit adjustments, and eventwear demand remaining healthy. The main downside risks are apparel deflation in some categories, cheap replacement garments, weak officewear demand, rent pressure and a limited pipeline of skilled sewing labor. Operators with appointment systems, transparent pricing, fast turnaround, pickup/delivery and relationships with bridal shops, boutiques, dry cleaners or resale stores are positioned better than purely walk-in neighborhood shops.
themes: Competition from dry cleaners and retailers
